Useful Memories Become Faulty
When Continuously Updated by LLMs

Dylan Zhang Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign    Yanshan Lin Affiliation: IIIS, Tsinghua University, Work done at UIUC    Zhengkun Wu Affiliation: IIIS, Tsinghua University, Work done at UIUC    Yihang Sun Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign    Bingxuan Li Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign    Dianqi Li Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign    Hao Peng Corresponding author: Dylan Zhang; shizhuo2@illinois.edu Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
Abstract

Learning from past experience benefits from two complementary forms of memory: episodic traces—raw trajectories of what happened—and consolidated abstractions distilled across many episodes into reusable, schema-like lessons. Recent agentic-memory systems pursue the consolidated form: an LLM rewrites past trajectories into a textual memory bank that it continuously updates with new interactions, promising self-improving agents without parameter updates. Yet we find that such consolidated memories produced by today’s LLMs are often faulty even when derived from useful experiences. As consolidation proceeds, memory utility first rises, then degrades, and can fall below the no-memory baseline. More surprisingly, even when consolidating from ground-truth solutions, GPT-5.4 fails on 54% of a set of ARC-AGI problems it had previously solved without memory. We trace the regression to the consolidation step rather than the underlying experience: the same trajectories yield qualitatively different memories under different update schedules, and an episodic-only control that simply retains those trajectories remains competitive with the consolidators we test. In a controlled ARC-AGI Stream environment that exposes Retain, Delete, and Consolidate actions, agents preserve raw episodes by default and double the accuracy of their forced-consolidation counterparts; disabling consolidation entirely (episodic management only) matches this auto regime. Practically, robust agent memory should treat raw episodes as first-class evidence and gate consolidation explicitly rather than firing it after every interaction. Looking forward, reliable agentic memory will require LLMs that can consolidate without overwriting the evidence they depend on.

1 Introduction

Memory consolidation is the cognitive process by which individual experiences are stabilized, reorganized, and integrated into long-term memory over time. Rather than preserving every episode as a raw record, consolidation helps extract recurring patterns, discard incidental details, and connect new information with existing knowledge. A central hallmark of intelligence is the ability to turn repeated experience into reusable knowledge. Humans do not treat every new situation as entirely unfamiliar; instead, they gradually summarize common structure from past episodes and organize it into abstractions through memory consolidation (McClelland et al., 1995; Squire et al., 2015; Dudai et al., 2015; Moscovitch et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2023; Bartlett, 1932). These consolidated abstractions allow humans to transfer lessons learned in one context to novel but related situations, enabling efficient reasoning, faster adaptation, and more robust generalization beyond the exact events they have previously encountered.

Recent agentic-memory systems pursue a similar idea for LLM agents. After solving a problem, an agent can distill its trajectory into a textual abstraction of the skill it has learned, store this abstraction in persistent memory, and refine it as more related problems are encountered (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Sumers et al., 2024; Park et al., 2023; Majumder et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026; Ouyang et al., 2026). This paradigm is especially appealing because it suggests a practical path toward self-evolving agents: Experience can be accumulated, compressed, and reused as compact textual knowledge, without requiring any parameter updates.

In this work, we systematically examine what happens when agents repeatedly compress past trajectories into memory and reuse that memory over long horizons. To make the experiences themselves informative by construction, we study settings in which the input trajectories are demonstrably useful: either drawn from problems the agent has already solved without memory, or supplied with ground-truth solutions. Even under these favorable conditions, we find that current LLMs are not reliable memory consolidators. Each consolidation step is a lossy rewrite of the memory store: useful details are dropped, spurious rules are introduced, and once-helpful abstractions drift away from the underlying task structure. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop (Yao et al., 2022), AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024), and a controlled testbed we introduce to make consolidation failures more visible, agents that incrementally abstract their accumulating trajectories into a textual memory bank can briefly improve or plateau before degrading—in some cases falling below the same agents without memory at all (Fig. 1(a)). The clearest case isolates the consolidation step from any input-side excuse: GPT-5.4 first solves a set of ARC-AGI problems at 100%100\% accuracy with no memory; after consolidating from ground-truth solutions to those very problems, it then fails on 46%46\% of them (Fig. 2). The failure can therefore be attributed to faulty memory rather than to noisy trajectories.

Consolidation is fragile in a second sense: the same set of trajectories can yield qualitatively different memories depending on the order and grouping of updates. Consolidating the whole trajectory pool in one pass (Static-All) versus streaming it batch-by-batch (Stream) produces different end states (Fig. 3); updates on one task overwrite memory of another (Figs. 8(b) and 8(c)); and a stream of repeated near-duplicates causes the memory to overfit to seen instances and generalize poorly within the same task (Fig. 11). Meanwhile, an episodic-only control that consumes the same trajectories without abstracting them—appending raw rollouts to context as in-context demonstrations—is already competitive with the lesson-style consolidators we test (Table 2). Because the trajectory pool is held fixed across these comparisons, the variance across schedules and the episodic-only control together point to the consolidation step itself, not the underlying experience, as the source of the failure.

We further identify three mechanisms behind faulty memory (§6). First, agents misgroup experiences before abstracting them, pooling episodes that do not share underlying structure. Second, even when grouping is correct, abstraction can strip the applicability conditions of a lesson, so that overgeneralized entries interfere with neighboring tasks. Third, when the input stream is narrow, abstraction overfits to seen instances. Together, these failure modes weaken the boundary between what should be generalized, what should remain task-specific, and what should be preserved as raw episodic evidence (Sun et al., 2023; Bartlett, 1932; Brainerd and Reyna, 2002).

These findings suggest a limitation in current LLM agents: while they can often benefit from individual past episodes, they do not reliably turn those episodes into stable and reusable abstractions over long horizons. Many recent agentic-memory systems—CLIN (Majumder et al., 2023), Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al., 2024), Dynamic Cheatsheet (Suzgun et al., 2026), and ACE (Zhang et al., 2025)—adopt update-after-every-interaction designs that treat each consolidation step as at worst neutral; our results contradict this assumption. For today’s models, retaining episodes is the more robust default: when ARC-AGI Stream agents are given retain, delete, and consolidate actions, they preserve episodes by default and outperform their forced-consolidation counterparts. Yet episodic accumulation cannot be the long-term answer: as deployment continues, raw histories grow unboundedly and resist compositional reuse—compression and transfer ultimately require abstraction. We see faulty memory as a central open problem in agentic memory, and our results motivate architectures that keep the episodic and abstraction-forming roles distinct rather than collapsing both into a single rewrite loop.

2 Background and Related Work

Memory in LLM agents.

LLM agents augment fixed-weight models with editable textual memory that they themselves maintain. Across architectures, this memory takes many forms: hierarchical context stores (Packer et al., 2023; Letta, 2024), reflective notes (Shinn et al., 2023), episodic streams (Park et al., 2023), distilled lessons (Zhao et al., 2024), skill libraries (Wang et al., 2023), causal abstractions (Majumder et al., 2023), dynamic memory stores (Chhikara et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; LangChain AI, 2024), evolving playbooks (Zhang et al., 2025), dynamic cheatsheets (Suzgun et al., 2026), and reasoning memory banks (Ouyang et al., 2026). A popular paradigm is that LLMs abstract useful procedural information from experience into text. This work mainly concerns that category.

Schema formation and metacognitive control.

Cognitive theories of memory describe two complementary processes: a fast episodic system that stores individual experiences, and a slow process that extracts compact schemas—abstractions over many episodes that integrate with prior knowledge to support future generalization (McClelland et al., 1995; Squire et al., 2015; Dudai et al., 2015; Moscovitch et al., 2016). Schema formation is beneficial when new evidence fits existing structure (Tse et al., 2007), but harmful when it is non-selective or poorly controlled: nonselective consolidation causes interference and loss of specificity (McClelland et al., 1995; Sun et al., 2023). Whether consolidation helps therefore depends on metacognitive control—deciding which experiences belong together, how abstractly to rewrite them, and when to preserve distinctions rather than collapse them. Human metacognition is itself imperfect (Flavell, 1979; Nelson and Narens, 1990; Koriat, 1997), and whether LLMs reliably monitor their self-generated abstractions is an open question—in adjacent settings, chain-of-thought explanations have been shown to diverge from the underlying computation (Turpin et al., 2023). Agent-memory systems implement an explicit analogue, abstracting “lessons” that are reused on later tasks while putting the same model in charge of both generating the memory and monitoring its own abstraction; the failure modes we observe (§6) are consistent with this control loop being unreliable in practice.

3 Experiment Set-up

We study how models abstract memory from experience across clean and widely-used agent benchmarks—ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024), and Mind2Web (Deng et al., 2023)—and a synthetic stream we built, ARC-AGI Stream, to introspect the memory-management process under known task families and ground-truth solutions.

We adopt representative agentic-memory methods that distill lessons from past trajectories—CLIN (Majumder et al., 2023), Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al., 2024), Dynamic Cheatsheet (Suzgun et al., 2026), and ACE (Zhang et al., 2025).

Memory construction conditions.

Three regimes differ only in how trajectories are presented to the memory manager: Static-All abstracts memory from the entire pool in one-shot; Static-Group does so for each task type (for ALFWorld and ScienceWorld) and concatenate: this simulates offline memory construction and is used for control; Stream updates in batches, simulating an agent that evolves continually. For Stream we change batch size and within-batch task composition (homogeneous vs. heterogeneous) and consider both unbounded and size-capped memory banks. At evaluation we provide all memory entries in context and average two repeats per question unless noted otherwise.

ARC-AGI Stream.

We introduce ARC-AGI Stream, a controlled testbed for introspecting the abstraction process itself rather than only its downstream accuracy. Building on ARCGEN (Moffitt, 2025), the testbed combines three properties that, jointly, are absent from existing agent benchmarks: (i) a fully specified latent task taxonomy—following ConceptARC (Moskvichev et al., 2023), each concept is a distinct problem type, so memory-management actions (Fig. 7(a)) and results (Fig. 6) can be traced family-by-family. (ii) programmatic ground-truth and (iii) an exposed, structured vocabulary of memory operations whose use we can audit per step. These controls make abstraction errors attributable: if a model receives correct episodes from known families but later merges families, the failure lies in memory abstraction rather than others. Together they enable the family-coverage, misclassification, and buffer-composition analyses in §6 that would not be measurable on ALFWorld/ScienceWorld/WebShop. Following the Complementary Learning Systems framing (McClelland et al., 1995; Sun et al., 2023; Tse et al., 2007), we maintain two stores: an Episodic buffer of problem –solution pairs and an Abstract store of consolidated lessons; the control conditions below are designed to test this gating prediction directly. At each step the model may Retain a raw episode, Delete an entry, or Consolidate buffered episodes into the Abstract store; the solver can be conditioned on either store or both stores. We compare three control loops: Force requires consolidation each round and no Episodic entries persist between rounds; Auto lets the model choose whether to retain raw or abstract; Episodic Management Only allows only retention and deletion, disabling abstraction entirely. Two trajectory regimes complete the design: GT, where ground-truth solutions are streamed to simulate training on demonstrations, and Running, where the agent learns from its own attempts as it solves new problems. Prompt templates are documented in Appendix B; the family and skill taxonomy used by the generator is in Appendix A.

4 Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs

4.1 Stream Updates Reveal The Cumulative Effect Of Imperfect Abstraction

Abstracted memory utility is non-monotonic in updates.

Starting from an empty memory store, abstracted-memory utility rises early and then falls below the no-memory baseline as updates accumulate. Figure 1(a) shows this curve on ScienceWorld with batches of 4 trajectories: the score peaks near step 20 and declines through step 100 for every memory size and sometimes below no-memory baseline. The same shape recurs on WebShop, where AWM goes from 0.640.64 at 88 examples to 0.200.20 at 128128 while no-memory sits at 0.200.20 (Fig. 1(b))—scaling the memory eventually erases its own benefit.

A strong memory is not a fixed point.

A high-quality starting memory does not stabilize under continued consolidation either. We first consolidate ALFWorld trajectories with GPT-5.4—the strongest model we test—following the Static-Group setting from §3, then continue updating that store in batches with GPT-5-nano on the same trajectory pool. Evaluated under three solvers (Qwen3.5-{27B, 9B, 4B}) to avoid idiosyncraticy, utility declines across all three solvers and can drop drastically between consecutive evaluation steps (Fig. 4).

The agent regresses on tasks it has already solved.

The cleanest, most striking instance is in-distribution regression on a 19-problem slice of the ARC-AGI Stream that GPT-5.4 solves at 100%100\% accuracy without memory. Streaming those same problems through the consolidation loop, with ground-truth solutions available at every step, brings GPT-5.4 down to 54%54\% on the very problems it had previously solved (Fig. 2).

The consolidation procedure itself shapes the rate of decline.

The decline is not driven by content alone; how trajectories are presented to the consolidator changes the resulting memory in content-independent ways. 1. Grouping by task family helps. Holding update strategy fixed, consolidating each task family separately (Static-Group) outperforms consolidating across families jointly (Static-All - marked as Ungrp.); pooling heterogeneous tasks into a single abstraction step invites confusion between unrelated procedures (Fig. 3). 2. One-shot consolidation beats streaming. Holding the trajectory pool fixed, Streamed incremental updates underperform a single whole-pool pass (Fig. 3). This suggests that early abstractions can anchor later rewrites and mistakes are reused as context for future consolidation, so small errors in segmentation or abstraction compound into progressively distorted memories. However, in continual learning loops, memory gets repeatedly updated as agents collect more experiences, instead of seeing the entire pool of past interactions, precisely falling to the lossy update regime.

3. Heterogeneous batches accelerate the decline within streaming. Even when updates must be streamed, batches that mix tasks produce worse memory than batches drawn from one task at a time (Fig. 4): the model merges incompatible lessons inside a single update.

Implications for memory design.

Each abstraction pass is a lossy rewrite that compounds over updates. The pattern makes two predictions for how memory should be organized, which §5 tests directly. (i) The raw trajectory logs that the consolidator distills from should remain a competitive baseline, since they retain what each rewrite discards. (ii) Allowing an agent to keep raw episodes alongside (or instead of) abstracting them should outperform a regime that forces every trajectory through consolidation.

4.2 An episodic-only store should be a diagnostic baseline

In WebShop, ALFWorld and AppWorld, an episodic-only memory—append-only trajectory rollouts in context, with no cross-trajectory abstraction —is competitive with lesson-style consolidator we test (Table 2; WebShop in Table 3 in Appendix). The trajectory baseline stores the same experience that ACE, AWM, and Dynamic Cheatsheet are asked to compress, and all memory entries are placed in context at evaluation.

In most cases, abstracted memory cannot significantly outperform direct in-context learning from trajectory logs (or subsets of them). It means the evidence available before abstraction already contains task-relevant signal that the solver can exploit directly: observations, actions, intermediate failures, and environmental feedback remain tied to the concrete situation in which they occurred. Schema-like behavior can emerge from in-context learning on preserved instances comparative to a separately stored abstraction (Hintzman, 1986; Brooks, 1978; Medin and Schaffer, 1978; Logan, 1988). Therefore, we suggest that a memory method whose value depends on distillation should be tested against the unabstracted rollouts it distills.

5 Mitigating Faulty Abstraction

The findings in § 4 imply experiences contain information the LLMs can consume for better task performance, but the challenge is that those information fades with repeated LLM updates instead of being refined.

Therefore, the memory architecture should be allowed to preserve episodes instead of forcing every new experience through consolidation. In this section, we present a controlled study to test whether granting models autonomy of retention versus abstraction, and allowing parallel stores of abstract and episodic memory would be a mitigation to the effect.

ARC-AGI Stream lets us instantiate the two-process design explicitly. The agent maintains both an Episodic buffer and an Abstract store, and at each step may Retain, Delete, or Consolidate (Auto; cf. § 3). We compare this to Force, where consolidation is required at every round and no episodic entry persists between rounds. Three observations follow.

First, the episodic store carries most of the gain. Removing episodic evidence and using only abstract lessons collapses accuracy back to the no-memory baseline (Fig. 9(a)), indicating that the useful information was retained in raw episodes rather than distilled entries.

Second, Episodic Management Only—retention and deletion of raw episodes with abstraction disabled—matches or exceeds the full Auto mode (Fig. 9(a)). In this regime, the agent’s gains do not require an abstract store at all.

Third, forced abstraction underperforms retained-episode policies. Across 400400 training steps, Auto—which keeps episodes by default and uses abstraction sparingly—generally outperforms Force on both backbones we test (Fig. 5). Whatever Force gains from compression, it can lose more by overwriting evidence.

The agent’s own management decisions point in the same direction. Given the option, it saturates the episodic buffer quickly at both budget levels while keeping the abstract store sparse (Fig. 7(b)). The Auto-mode result therefore reflects an episodic-first policy that the agent chooses when the architecture permits it.

Principle.

Episodic and schema-forming roles should not be collapsed into a single rewrite loop. Complementary Learning Systems make this prescription explicitly: a fast episodic store and a slow schema-forming store are kept architecturally distinct so that fast learning does not overwrite the slow one, and consolidation is gated by schema fit rather than triggered on every event (McClelland et al., 1995; Kumaran et al., 2016; Tse et al., 2007; Sun et al., 2023). The Force regime collapses this separation into a mandatory rewrite loop, recreating the interference conditions the dual-system design was meant to prevent (McCloskey and Cohen, 1989; French, 1999). An episodic store should therefore retain the evidence; abstraction, when it happens, should be opt-in and gated by the agent rather than forced on every trajectory.

In our experiments, both policies that gate abstraction (Auto) and policies that disable it entirely (Episodic Management Only) match or exceed forced abstraction (Force), pointing to mandatory rewriting at every step—rather than abstraction itself—as the decisive failure mode in this regime (Nelson and Narens, 1990; Koriat, 1997).

6 Failure Modes

We introspect three abstraction failures both quantitatively and qualitatively: misgrouping before abstraction, interference from overgeneralized lessons, and overfit to narrow streams of examples. We present full case study results in Appendix D.

6.1 Correct Segmentation Takes Time, Forced Abstraction Breaks It

Correct segmentation—identifying which experiences belong together before abstraction—is a precondition: an agent cannot abstract a lesson from a set of episodes it has failed to group correctly (Zacks et al., 2007).

The capacity for correct segmentation is in fact present. Given autonomy over its memory, the model eventually converges to a clean episodic store covering each of the 6 problem types(Fig. 6). Yet the process takes time: only after 71 steps (568 examples) does the model admit all six problem types into the buffer. In the Force regime, where the model must consolidate at every step (8 fresh examples), it makes mistakes frequently. Figure 7(a) reports the misclassification count — the number of memory-management actions that combine episodes from two or more distinct problem classes — and shows that, under forced consolidation, the model routinely merges across class boundaries. The bottleneck is not recognizing class structure but preserving it through cross-episode abstraction: the forced act of abstraction overrides the segmentation the model is otherwise capable of.

6.2 Interference

Each abstraction pass smooths and abstracts existing entries—a process analogous to the semanticization of episodic memories under repeated retelling (Bartlett, 1932); when the underlying chunks are imprecisely bounded, this abstraction strips the preconditions under which a lesson applies, leaving what reads as broadly relevant when it is not. On a related but different problem (Pick&Place versus Pick-Clean-Place in ALFWorld), the agent sees these overgeneralized lessons and is misled rather than aided (Fig. 8(c)).

The same interference dynamic shows up at the entire learning run level under task switching. On the 15-task ScienceWorld switch sequence, we compare two abstraction set-ups at each task tt: Fresh, which distills memories only on task tt, against Cumulative, which consolidates jointly over tasks …​t1\!\dots\!t. Cumulative ends +203+203 points behind Fresh (Fig. 10). We use LLM judge to label each memory entry and find Cumulative accumulates over-generalized memories at ∼5×\sim\!5\times Fresh’s rate and garbage memories at ∼20×\sim\!20\times, with both gaps widening monotonically across the 15 tasks (App. K.2, Fig. 18).

6.3 Overfit

A complementary failure mode emerges when the input distribution narrows rather than widens. In our ARC-AGI experiments, we repeatedly feed the model tasks drawn from a single strategy family across consolidation cycles. As the iteration count grows, the memory overfits to the specific instances it has seen: performance remains stable on exact repetitions of those problems but collapses on simple variations within the same strategy family (Fig. 11; see Appendix D for case studies).

The abstraction loop, given a narrow stream, abstracts toward the surface regularities of the observed instances rather than the underlying problem-solving strategy.

Case Study

We ground the failures above in concrete memory artifacts across four environments: ARC-AGI strategy-memory pathologies (Appendix D), ALFWorld memorycollapse (Appendix G), WebShop AWM collapse-by-accretion (Section H.1.2), and ScienceWorld abnormal-memory categories (Section J.1). A memory surgery ablation isolates their content-level bite: removing a single workflow (W8) from a WebShop consolidated memory raises pass rate (Section I.1), since W8 biases the agent toward click[Next >] dead loops at the expense of click[Buy Now].

7 Conclusion

Persistent memory is meant to let LLM agents move beyond static competence: experience is stored, compressed into reusable lessons, and carried forward. We identify an issue that may undermine this promise — across agent benchmarks and ARC-AGI Stream, continuously updated textual memory can become less useful as experience accumulates; in the cleanest case, an agent becomes worse on the very problems its memory was built from.

The failure lies in the consolidation loop itself. Current LLMs do not reliably decide which episodes belong together, which distinctions should survive compression, or when an experience should remain episodic. They misgroup trajectories, overgeneralize lessons, and overfit to narrow streams. Because each update rewrites the products of earlier updates, small abstraction errors compound into faulty memory.

These findings suggest that raw episodes should be treated as first-class evidence, not disposable material to be compressed away. Abstraction should be selective, delayed, and grounded in recoverable trajectories. Until agents can control when and how to consolidate experience, continuously updated textual memory should be treated not as a reliable engine of self-improvement, but as a fragile mechanism that can make more experience produce worse memory.

8 Limitations

Our study has several scope conditions. First, we evaluate text-based agentic benchmarks (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, AppWorld, Mind2Web) and a controlled ARC-AGI Stream environment; whether the same erosion dynamics appear in embodied, multi-modal, or tool-rich production settings remains open. Second, we study natural-language abstraction as implemented by contemporary LLMs (GPT-5.4 family and Qwen3.5 family); parametric memory (weight updates, distillation into the model) and structured non-textual memory representations are out of scope. Third, the consolidator and the solver are themselves LLMs, so faulty abstraction reflects current model capability and could shift with stronger consolidators or with consolidator- specific fine-tuning. Fourth, due to API-cost constraints we report point estimates from a small number of repeats per question rather than formal error bars; we mitigate this by checking that conclusions hold across multiple models, benchmarks, and memory frameworks, but per-figure variance should be interpreted with this in mind.

9 Broader Impacts

Our findings are diagnostic: they identify a failure mode in a widely adopted paradigm for agent memory and suggest more conservative default designs that preserve raw evidence and gate abstraction. The positive impact is to reduce silent regressions in deployed long-horizon agents and to direct research toward more reliable abstraction mechanisms. Negative impacts are indirect: better long-horizon agent memory could amplify the reach of autonomous systems whose downstream uses (persuasion, automation of consequential decisions) carry their own risks, and our diagnosis of failure modes does not constitute a fix. We do not release new datasets or models that pose specific misuse concerns, and the benchmarks we use are public.

Appendix A Family and skill taxonomy [ARC-AGI]

This section defines the two terms “family” and “skill” and lists the six families and seven skills used in the ARC-AGI experiments.

A.1 Definitions

Our task generator decomposes an ARC-style task along two independent axes:

  • •

    Family: a rule that selects the subset of connected non-background objects in the input grid that participates in the task’s transformation.

  • •

    Skill: a fixed transformation applied to each selected object.

The two axes are orthogonal: the same family can be paired with different skills, and the same skill can be paired with different families. Some families are adapted from concept groups in ConceptARC; for example, detect_inside_frame_relation corresponds to the InsideOutside concept group.

A.2 Family catalog

The six families span five distinct selection criteria: two are based on intrinsic per-object attributes (color, size extremum), one on a global conditional cue (a marker cell that triggers a branch), one on a cross-object relation (shape-frequency mode), one on a spatial containment relation (objects strictly inside a frame), and one on a cross-grid structural property (a sub-scene of a two-panel input). The chosen skill is then applied uniformly to whichever objects the family selects.

Figure 12 shows one task per family under a fixed skill of recolor: recolored objects in the output identify the family’s selection by color contrast.

A.3 Skill catalog

Each skill applies a fixed transformation to every object in the family’s selection.

Figure 13 shows the per-skill effect under a fixed family of detect_color_property, where the selection is visually simple (objects whose color matches a target predicate demonstrated by the examples), isolating the skill’s per-object action.

Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI]

The experiments use three prompts: a solver prompt issued once per task, a consolidator decision prompt that selects an action on the recent history buffer after each passing step, and a consolidator extraction prompt that produces a replacement strategy memory from a selected subset of history. To make every field concrete we reproduce one full step from a real run in which the current solve passes; the history buffer carries two prior passing trajectories and strategy memory holds one entry distilled at an earlier step. Each prompt is shown together with the response it elicited. Where long content repeats across prompts (the eight extra IO examples for the current task; the 8 tool-buffer helper bodies; grids and solve code already shown above), we mark the elision in square brackets; everything else is byte-for-byte from the run logs.

B.1 Solver prompt

The solver prompt is issued once per task at the start of the step. It bundles the 10 IO examples for the current task, the existing strategy memory, the tool-buffer helper signatures, and the recent history buffer into one call.

An alternative invocation pattern for the solver decomposes the call into a strategy-selection step followed by a synthesis step. The selection prompt provides three inputs: the current callable helper buffer, half of the task’s input-output examples, and the current strategy memory. The model replies with a JSON object that names which existing entry to apply; in the unconstrained variant it may instead propose a new one. Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI]

C.1 How a strategy is traced across compress steps

At each compress step we run the extraction prompt (section B.4); the consolidator returns the rewritten strategy memory as a JSON list. Each list item declares its kind, one of three values:

  • •

    retain — keep an existing entry from the current memory; the field from_existing lists 1-based indices into that memory.

  • •

    new — distill a fresh entry from selected input tasks; the field from_functions lists 1-based indices into this step’s input tasks.

  • •

    merge — emit a new entry that combines existing entries (from_existing) with new input tasks (from_functions).

Both kind and the two index fields come directly from the consolidator’s JSON output. After parsing the response, we persist the resulting memory as a per-step JSON snapshot; each entry in the snapshot carries this step’s kind and its associated indices.

Because both merge and new produce a fresh entry rather than editing an existing one in place, tracking how a strategy evolves over multiple steps requires walking from_existing pointers backwards across snapshots. Starting from a target entry, we look at its kind: if kind = new, the chain has reached its root and the walk terminates; if kind = merge, the index from_existing: [j] points to a predecessor in the previous compress step’s memory; we look up the predecessor in the snapshot we persisted for that step and take it as the new target. We call a chain reconstructed by this procedure a strategy lineage.

C.2 Worked lineage example

We ran GPT-5.4 on a 200-task pool spanning six ARC families, with the same model serving as both solver and consolidator. We trace one strategy lineage by the procedure of section C.1, from its new step through its final merge, and show three snapshots: the chain root, an intermediate node, and the chain’s final node. In the latter two, yellow shading marks spans that differ from the previous snapshot.

Chain root.

The chain begins with a new step: the consolidator distills four inside-frame tasks into one entry.

Intermediate node.

Compared with the chain root: the horizontal-flip coordinate formula at root step (7) is gone, the When to use clause about mirroring is gone, and a uniform-recolor step has been added in its place. The overall scaffold — identify the frame as the largest object, classify other objects by strict bounding-box containment, erase the frame and outside objects, keep the inside objects — is preserved nearly verbatim.

Chain end.

Compared with the previous snapshot: the recolor step is gone, replaced by a uniform-translation step at the same position, and the When to use now mentions all shifted by one common offset in line with that change. The mirror clause that was already missing in the previous snapshot is still absent.

Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI]

Each subsection below names one failure mode and shows a verbatim entry from the strategy memory, paired with either a callout that explains highlighted spans or a held-out solver code comparison.

D.1 Vacuous abstraction

We ran GPT-5-mini on a 200-task pool spanning six families. After each task, the model could update its strategy memory or leave it unchanged; we set no cap on entry count. After task 200, the memory’s first entry read:

D.2 Concrete-vocabulary erosion

We showed GPT-5-mini one training task (“recolor the largest object”) for 50 consecutive rewrites of its memory. Round 1 still mentions “max size” — the only concrete property the task actually selects on — as a parenthetical example of the metric to compute. By round 50, the same lineage has no word left for it:

D.3 Foreign-family injection

We presented training tasks to GPT-5.4 one at a time, each paired with its ground-truth solver code. We required the model to compress every task into a single memory entry on receipt. The compressor distilled the task into an entry whose Strategy steps mix in content from multiple families.

D.4 Phantom strategies from failed attempts

In a 200-task GPT-5.4 run, we exposed the strategy-update prompt to both successful and failed past attempts (each failure paired with the wrong output it produced). We expected this to let the model prune bad entries by surfacing what had not worked. The output instead distilled recurring patterns from the failed code into new entries. The strategy library at the end of the run held five entries; two were paraphrases of the same fictional rule. We reproduce the longer paraphrase below:

D.5 Single-strategy collapse on multi-family compression

The cases above describe entries whose content is itself problematic. This subsection describes a different failure with two parts: (i) compression collapses multi-family training tasks into one single-family playbook; (ii) retrieval applies that entry verbatim to held-out tasks from other families. The entry text itself is internally consistent and appropriate for its source family.

Example 1: 19 tasks revisited 10 times collapse to a single inside-frame plus hollow strategy.

We presented a fixed pool of 19 tasks, spanning the six families, to GPT-5.4 10 times. The model viewed one task at a time alongside its ground-truth solver code, and updated its memory after each task. After 10 passes (190 steps), the memory contained a single entry:

On a held-out task whose true rule was “erase every object of one specific color” — unrelated to the inside-frame pattern in the entry — the same model produced:

The first comment reproduces the entry’s framing verbatim. The second comment records the active color from the examples. The code below treats color 66 as the frame color rather than as the color to remove. The code follows the entry’s frame-and-inside structure: it picks a frame by size, copies only strictly-interior objects onto a blank canvas, and hollows them in place. On this input no color-33 marker passes the strict-inside check, so the canvas stays empty. The same model without strategy memory solved the task in eight lines:

Example 2: 250 tasks streamed once collapse to a group-by-shape strategy.

In a separate run, we presented 250 training tasks to GPT-5.4 one at a time, each paired with its ground-truth solver code. After each task the model chose whether to update the memory. Training tasks again spanned the six families. After 250 steps the memory contained two entries, both from the group-by-shape family. Each entry prescribed partitioning objects by translation-normalized shape signature, keeping the most frequent signature class, and applying a decoration to the survivors. The other five families (largest-object, color-property, key-marker, inside-frame, compose-horizontal) had no entry in the memory.

On a held-out task from the largest-object family — true rule “keep only the largest connected component, erase the rest” — the same model with this memory produced:

The solver transcribes the entry’s selection logic into Python: signature() implements step (2), the dictionary count implements step (3), and best_sig implements step (4). The downstream operation — writing each kept object’s cells onto a blank canvas — is identical to what the same model produces without memory, shown next:

Without memory the model identifies the correct selection criterion (obj["size"] == max_size). With memory the selection criterion is replaced by the entry’s signature(obj) == best_sig. The action that follows the selection is unchanged. Replacing the selection criterion alone, while keeping the action identical, drops the solver from 10/10 to 2/10 on this task’s 10 test grids.

Appendix F Additional Experiment Details

F.1 ALFWorld

Training data

We use trajectories on the six standard ALFWorld task types, generated by gpt-4.1 or gpt-5-nano (see table 7):

  • •

    pick_and_place

  • •

    pick_clean_then_place_in_recep

  • •

    pick_two_obj_and_place

  • •

    look_at_obj_in_light

  • •

    pick_cool_then_place_in_recep

  • •

    pick_heat_then_place_in_recep

We use script-normalized task names; the upstream ALFWorld task type for pick_and_place is pick_and_place_simple, with the _simple suffix stripped during data preparation.

“n=64n{=}64” and “n=128n{=}128” below refer to the number of trajectories per task type, so a n=64n{=}64 set contains 64×6=38464\times 6=384 trajectories in total. All rollouts use max_steps=50.

Three training-data variants are used across the experiments (table 7):

After collection, every raw trajectory is converted into a structured memory item via the abstraction step of the SkillRL pipeline. We use gpt-5.4 as the abstraction LLM. The abstraction makes 3 LLM calls per trajectory and produces one item with three fields: contextual_description, refined_trajectory, and strategic_guidelines.

Two-task-type probe set

For one probe experiment we use a focused training subset that pairs two task types: pick_and_place (focal) and pick_clean_then_place_in_recep (probe). The base memory at every probe point is a single-type consolidation that fixes the per-stage task type to pick_and_place and samples 32 abstracts per stage from the n=64n{=}64 abstract pool; snapshots are taken at consolidation stage S∈{1,20,50,100}S\in\{1,20,50,100\}. From each snapshot we run one additional consolidation iteration with 32 abstracts. The management model is gpt-5-nano and it has a max capacity of memory, which is 50.

Evaluation set

We evaluate on eval_id_balanced_48, a 48-episode subset of ALFWorld’s in-distribution test split with 8 episodes per task type for the 6 task types listed above.

Metric

Each ALFWorld episode has a binary success indicator (env reward =1=1 when the agent satisfies the goal within max_steps=50, else 0). We report wins/48 (the count of successful episodes) and the corresponding success rate in [0,1][0,1] as the per-condition score on this evaluation set.

F.2 WebShop

Training data

WebShop training data come in two variants (table 8).

Golden 128. We sample 128 trajectories (seed =42=42) from the WebShop subset of the AgentGym AgentTraj-L corpus, filtered to score =1.0=1.0 (perfect-reward demonstrations only). We replay these trajectories through our WebShop environment instance (num_products=1000) using a replay script that re-executes each AgentGym action sequence to obtain matching raw trajectories. The 128 sampled tasks are drawn sparsely from AgentGym’s success-filtered train pool; their underlying WebShop session identifiers span the range 7272–67726772 (sparse; 128 distinct IDs). This is the training set used for the AWM-style Workflow 8 ablation in section I.1.

Non-golden 128. We use a separate, contiguous block of 128 WebShop sessions (session IDs 15001500–16271627), disjoint from the test pool [0,500)[0,500). On these sessions we collect 128 trajectories generated by gpt-5.4-mini directly, with no reward filtering. Most resulting trajectories have score <1.0<1.0 (table 8). This set tests how memory consolidation behaves when the input training trajectories are themselves imperfect.

After collection, raw trajectories are abstracted into structured memory items via the same SkillRL abstraction pipeline used for ALFWorld.

Evaluation set

We evaluate on test50_seed42_no_leak.json, a 50-session subset of WebShop’s test pool (num_products=1000, seed =42=42) drawn from the index range [0,500)[0,500). The 13 training-set session IDs (all from Golden 128) that fall within [0,500)[0,500) are excluded from the sampling pool before drawing. Final session indices span 33–467467.

Metric

Each WebShop episode terminates with a reward in [0,1][0,1] computed from attribute match between the purchased product and the instruction (a perfect match yields reward 1.01.0). If the agent never issues a click[Buy Now] action and the episode ends without a purchase (e.g., the agent times out at eval_max_steps), the reward is 00. We report two quantities per condition: wins/50 (the count of episodes with reward =1.0=1.0) and mean reward (arithmetic mean of episode rewards over the 50 evaluation sessions).

F.3 ScienceWorld

We select 15 medium-difficulty tasks from ScienceWorld for the memory consolidation experiments, where each selected task satisfies an average optimal action sequence length between 20 and 100. In total, these tasks contain 485 rollout cases. The task names and the number of rollout cases for each task are shown in Table 9.

Our ScienceWorld experiments are based on the CLIN setting, with several adaptations for studying long-horizon memory consolidation. Following CLIN, each rollout is presented together with an evaluation report (1), which provides feedback about the success or failure of the corresponding attempt. We also follow the CLIN-style constrained memory format (2), where each memory is written as a unified natural-language rule using one of a small set of relation phrases, such as MAY BE NECCESSARY to, SHOULD BE NECCESSARY to, MAY BE CONTRIBUTE to, and DOES NOT CONTRIBUTE to.

Compared with the original CLIN update procedure, we introduce several modifications. First, we maintain a bounded memory bank and explicitly inform the LLM of the maximum memory-bank size and FIFO replacement policy, as highlighted in the memory-capacity instruction (3). Second, instead of only adding new memories, we allow multiple memory-bank operations, including delete (4), replace (5), add (6), and retain (7). Third, we feed rollouts to the LLM in mini-batches and ask the model to compare the buffered rollouts jointly before editing the memory bank, as shown in the mini-batch consolidation instruction (8). Finally, after each full pass over all rollouts for a given number of consolidation rounds, we evaluate the current memory bank on a fixed ScienceWorld test set. This test set contains 44 cases sampled from the same 15 selected tasks, with 2–4 cases per task depending on the number of available variants.

F.4 AppWorld

Training data

We use 140 trajectories collected on AppWorld’s official train and dev splits (Trivedi et al., 2024) as the shared training set across all memory-induction methods evaluated in this work.

The 90-task train segment uses AppWorld’s officially released ReAct baseline trajectories, produced with GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-05-13). The 50-task dev segment uses ReAct trajectories collected with Qwen3.5-27B on a stratified-by-difficulty sample of the dev split, run under AppWorld’s standard ReAct interface. Composition is summarized in table 10. The mean Task Goal Completion (TGC) over the combined 140 trajectories is 61.4%61.4\% (86/14086/140): 52.2%52.2\% on the train segment and 78.0%78.0\% on the dev segment.

For methods that require gold-quality input, we additionally collect a parallel set of 140 trajectories on the same task IDs by replaying AppWorld’s released ground-truth solutions through the environment API, yielding a 100%100\%-pass training set with identical task IDs and ordering.

Each training datapoint consists of a task identifier, a final pass/fail outcome, and a Qwen3.5-27B–generated prose summary of the full ReAct trajectory (thoughts, actions, and observations of all steps), used in place of the raw token-level trajectory to keep per-entry length tractable for prompt-time concatenation.

Evaluation set

We evaluate on a 100-task subset drawn from AppWorld’s two official test splits (test_normal with 168168 tasks and test_challenge with 417417) by proportional stratified sampling on difficulty: 50 tasks from each split, seed =42=42, with no overlap. All conditions are evaluated on the same 100 task IDs.

Metric

Each AppWorld task is paired with a set of Python unit tests. The official evaluator replays the agent’s trajectory against the resulting database state and runs these tests; a task is counted as a success only when all of its unit tests pass. Following AppWorld’s official protocol, we report Task Goal Completion (TGC) as the sole metric: the percentage of evaluation tasks whose success indicator equals one. All TGC values reported in the main tables are arithmetic means over the 100 evaluation tasks.

Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes

G.1 Erosion: good memory degrading over time

Setup.

The memory under study is produced by a 200-stage iterative consolidation run on ALFWorld. The base memory at stage 0 is a 10-item seed obtained by passing all 768 abstracts of the n=128n{=}128 golden ALFWorld training set (section F.1) through a single gpt-5.4 consolidation call that emits a free-count list of task-type-agnostic insights; the model picks the count, with no fixed target. Each subsequent stage feeds gpt-5-nano a fresh mini-batch of 66 abstracts (11 per task type, drawn from the n=64n{=}64 subset of the same six-type pool) together with the current memory; the management model rewrites the entire memory at every stage and forces overwrites rather than appends. Besides, the memory capacity is 50. We evaluate the consolidated memory at every 20 stages on the held-out balanced ALFWorld split (defined in section F.1; n=48 episodes) using three Qwen3.5 sizes as rollout policies — Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B, and Qwen3.5-27B — with each model’s reasoning mode disabled (the “no-thinking” setting). The full memory is supplied in the prompt context at every step, so the rollout sees every item in every snapshot.

The erosion curve.

fig. 16 plots wins/48 for the three rollout sizes at all evaluated stages, against the corresponding no-memory baselines (15/48 for both 4B and 9B; 19/48 for 27B). All three sizes show the same qualitative pattern: an early peak followed by a general decline (with small recoveries) to stage 200. The 4B and 9B rollouts each gain a small bump at stage 20 (35/48 wins), then erode to 15/48 (4B) and 16/48 (9B). The 27B rollout’s peak is at stage 0 (41/48), so for the 27B rollout consolidation never helps; it erodes to 22/48 by stage 200. By stage 200 the gap to the no-memory baseline collapses for the 4B and 9B rollouts (Δ=0\Delta{=}0 and Δ=1\Delta{=}1 respectively); the 27B rollout retains a Δ=3\Delta{=}3 gap above its baseline (22/48 vs. 19/48). Memory size stays bounded at 38–50 items by the cap throughout, so the erosion is in content quality, not item count.

What is in the memory at the peak.

At stage 20 the 42 items each cover a distinct decision-relevant insight. We reproduce items 0–5 verbatim below; items 6–41 expand on this cover set with concrete recipes for heat/cool/clean tasks, look-at-light tasks, and multi-object planning.

What is in the memory after erosion.

At stage 200 the 38 items collapse onto a small number of overlapping templates. By keyword scan, 22 of the 38 items mention the desklamp, 28 mention multi-object handling, and 33 mention systematic room-by-room search; the templates overlap heavily (most items mention more than one). Items 3 and 5 are byte-identical. The concrete meta-strategies of stage 20 — the cooling-vs-heating asymmetry of item 3, the shuttle default of item 5, the recognize-task-type-early principle of item 0 — do not appear in concrete actionable form in any of the five representative items below, and a full scan of the 38 items finds none that retain the cooling-vs-heating asymmetry as a separable insight.

G.2 Collapsed memory: single-stage merge to one item

Setup.

The iterative-consolidation pipeline matches section G.1: gpt-5-nano management model, memory capacity is 50 items, the same six ALFWorld task types, and the same gpt-5.4 abstraction step. The per-stage data sampling differs in one respect. Each stage feeds the manager a mini-batch of 66 trajectories drawn from a single (randomly chosen) task type, rather than a flat sample across all six types. Rollout policies are the three Qwen3.5 sizes (Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-27B); the evaluation split is the same balanced ALFWorld split as in section G.1. We focus on the single-stage transition S=168→S=169S{=}168\to S{=}169 in this run.

The collapse event.

At stage 168168 the memory contains 5050 items totalling 48,50648{,}506 characters (i.e., the cap is saturated, average ∼\sim970970 characters per item). One consolidation step later, at stage 169169, the memory contains a single item of 1,9601{,}960 characters. The manager has merged 5050 structured items into one numbered “unified loop” that tries to cover every ALFWorld task type at once. The collapse is concentrated in this single stage. The preceding stage 167167 has 4949 items; the following stage 170170 already begins to rebuild (22 items, 3,4103{,}410 chars). table 11 reports the rollout-level effect of this single-stage transition under the three Qwen3.5 sizes, against the corresponding no-memory baselines. section G.2 reproduces the single stage-169169 item verbatim.

G.3 Useless memory items

We distinguish two failure modes for memory items that are syntactically well-formed but supply no decision-relevant information. Both modes survive across stages because nothing contradicts them, and both consume retrieval bandwidth without shifting the action distribution.

Overgeneralized.

Items whose recommendation applies to any state (“be careful”, “consider all options”, “plan ahead”). The clause names no observable cue and shifts no prior over candidate actions when retrieved.

We pull three verbatim items from an ExpeL iterative consolidation run on ALFWorld (n=64n{=}64 trajectories per task type, gpt-5.4 base model, gpt-5-nano management, 200 mini-batch consolidation stages) at stage 200200. The stage-200 memory has 9 active rules; we display the top-1, top-2, and a low-vote item (Item 7, vote =2=2; the lowest is Item 8 with vote =1=1).

Worked example: how an ExpeL highest-voted insight collapsed.

The same run produced Item 0 above by repeatedly applying ExpeL’s EDIT operation to the top slot. By stage 200200 the slot had accumulated 9999 AGREE/EDIT votes, which would naively suggest extreme value. The vote counter, however, increments on EDIT but is not reset when an EDIT replaces the underlying concept. The score therefore tracks slot edit-volume rather than current content quality. Tracing the slot through stages, its content was rewritten through at least three distinct concepts (section G.3).

The slot’s 9999 votes were earned across three different concepts (examine-with-Y interaction →\to generic action selection →\to tautology). At stage 200200 only the third concept is in the slot; the other ∼80\sim 80 votes were accumulated by predecessors that the EDIT operation has since overwritten. The vote score is therefore not a measure of the current rule’s value to the agent.

Overspecified.

Items so narrowly tied to a past trajectory state or to one (object, surface, appliance) tuple that they cannot transfer once that condition is not present. They survive in the cap because nothing contradicts them; they take up retrieval bandwidth on tasks they do not match.

We pull three verbatim items from an ACE iterative consolidation run on ALFWorld (6 abstracts sampled flat-randomly across all six task types per stage; n=128n{=}128 trajectories per type; analyzer dedup threshold 0.750.75; both reflector and curator == gpt-5.4-mini). Each item is an ADD operation recorded in the curator’s operation log. Reflector and curator are the two ACE roles: the reflector emits bullet candidates from each trajectory, the curator decides which are added to or modified in the running memory, and the analyzer merges any pair of items whose embedding similarity exceeds the dedup threshold.

Appendix H WebShop

H.1 Memory artifacts from prior methods

This section reproduces, verbatim, two memory artifacts from prior consolidation methods on WebShop (Yao et al., 2022). They are intended as concrete reference points for the failure-mode taxonomy in appendix G — not as quantitative comparisons. For each artifact, report: method version and configuration (model, rewrite cadence), WebShop split and seed, and the trajectory step or consolidation round at which the snapshot was taken.

H.1.1 Healthy snapshots: ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet

We display one mid-run snapshot per method, taken after enough consolidation has happened to populate the memory but before any visible degradation. Both runs use n=64n{=}64 trajectories from the golden WebShop set and gpt-5.4-mini as the consolidation model.

ACE healthy.

ACE keeps a flat list of bullet items grouped into named sections (Common mistakes to avoid, Problem-solving heuristics). At stage 100100 of a 192192-stage run with dedup threshold 0.750.75, the memory contains 3232 bullets totalling about 1414k characters. We reproduce one short bullet from each section.

Dynamic Cheatsheet healthy.

Dynamic Cheatsheet keeps a single living document and rewrites it after every trajectory. The document at stage 100100 of the same run is roughly 8.38.3k characters, organised under a Action patterns and interaction sequences heading with one <memory_item> per consolidated insight (each with <description>, <example>, and a Count field). We reproduce two consecutive <memory_item> blocks.

These two snapshots illustrate the methods’ design intent: ACE produces structured bullet lists with explicit failure-mode categories, while Dynamic Cheatsheet produces one continuously-edited document with embedded action templates and counter-examples. Both show concrete domain content (apparel, sizes, colour names, price thresholds) and avoid the empty-content / paraphrase failure modes of sections G.3 and G.1.

H.1.2 Collapsed memory: Agent Workflow Memory

Setup.

The artifact is the AWM-style consolidated workflow file at epoch 33 of the same training run that supplies the epoch-11 snapshot used in the W8 ablation of section I.1: 128128 golden WebShop trajectories (n=128n{=}128, all reward =1.0=1.0), gpt-5.4-mini consolidator, batch size 1616, 3 epochs. Epoch 11 contains 88 workflows (W1–W8 in section I.1); epoch 33 contains 1616 workflows (W1–W16 below). The first 88 workflows of epoch 33 share titles and substantive content with epoch 11 (W2–W6 and W8 are character-identical modulo trailing whitespace; W1 and W7 receive minor wording edits over the next two epochs). The additional W9–W16 are new entries the consolidator appended over those epochs.

The collapsed snapshot.

We list epoch 33’s 1616 workflow titles below. The eight W9–W16 entries (highlighted) are category-specific specialisations of W1–W7; none introduces a new control-flow pattern or stop criterion not already present in W1–W7. We treat this as collapsed by accretion: the cap of the consolidation pipeline does not bind here, but the consolidator nevertheless stores redundant restatements of the same templates.

Appendix I Memory surgery

We isolate the contribution of individual memory items to overall failure by removing one item from a memory snapshot and re-evaluating, holding the rollout policy and all other items fixed.

I.1 Workflow 8 ablation on WebShop

Setup.

The memory under study is a consolidated workflow file (8 workflows W1–W8, reproduced verbatim in section I.1) produced after one epoch of AWM-style consolidation. AWM-style consolidation abstracts each input trajectory into a workflow template that pairs a thought rationale with an action sequence; we ablate Workflow 8 (W8) of the resulting file. The training data are 128 expert (task reward 1.01.0) trajectories sampled from the AgentGym AgentTraj-L WebShop corpus (seed 4242). The eval split is a 50-session subset of WebShop’s test pool (seed 4242) with overlap to the training sessions removed. We construct two evaluation conditions on this split:

  • •

    Full memory: all 8 workflows.

  • •

    Memory minus W8: the 7 workflows from the same file with Workflow 8 removed (no other edits).

All conditions use eval_max_steps=30, eval_max_tokens=4096, and eval_num_runs=1. We do not set a temperature parameter. Each condition is evaluated under two rollout policies, gpt-5.4-mini and gpt-5-mini. The memory artifact is byte-identical across the two rollouts.

The WebShop action space used in table 13 groups raw click[…] actions into six categories by the type of UI element clicked:

  • •

    search: issue a query against the catalog, e.g., search[red running shoes size 10 < $60]. Returns a paginated list of product cards.

  • •

    click ASIN: open a product detail page from a search-result card by its ASIN (Amazon Standard Identification Number, a 10-character product code such as b09npml43m), e.g., click[b09npml43m]. This is the only way to inspect a product’s variants, price, attributes, and Buy Now button.

  • •

    click variant: select a required option on a product page before purchase, e.g., click[medium], click[b16-red]. Many products require one or more such selections; missing a required variant prevents reward 1.0 even if Buy Now succeeds.

  • •

    click [Next >]: advance to the next page of search results without opening any product, e.g., click[Next >], click[next &gt;]. We also count the symmetric paging primitives click[< Prev] here.

  • •

    click back: return to the search input from a results or product page, e.g., click[Back to Search], abandoning the current query.

  • •

    click [Buy Now]: commit to purchasing the currently configured product. Terminates the episode and yields the final reward in [0,1][0,1] based on attribute match against the instruction.

The consolidated memory.

The full saved memory file contains 8 workflows, W1–W8, reproduced verbatim below. The original file delimits each block with XML-style <think> and <action> tags; we render them as italic “Thought”/“Action sequence” labels for readability and otherwise preserve the text. Highlighted spans in W8 key into the paired annotations callout that follows.

Result.

table 12 reports per-condition outcomes; table 13 breaks down the action stream by category.

Behavioral evidence.

With W8 in context, click[Next >] dominates the action stream relative to product-page interactions and click[Buy Now]. Removing W8 reduces this concentration in both rollouts (n=50 episodes per cell, single run; no significance test). Under gpt-5.4-mini, observed page-turn counts are 421421 (full) and 181181 (minus W8), a ratio of 2.3×2.3\times; the count of distinct episodes that issue at least one click[Buy Now] is 14/5014/50 (full) and 21/5021/50 (minus W8). Under gpt-5-mini, page-turn counts are 559559 and 246246 (also 2.3×2.3\times); the Buy-Now-episode count is 28/5028/50 and 33/5033/50.

Appendix J ScienceWorld

J.1 Abnormal memories

J.1.1 Representative cases

We first present three representative abnormal memory cases identified in the ScienceWorld environment, one from each abnormality category. These cases illustrate qualitatively different failure modes in memory consolidation: over_generalization, where a memory abstracts from prior experience too broadly and may bias the agent toward inappropriate actions; over_specialization, where a memory is tied to overly specific entities or procedures and therefore has limited transferability; and useless_garbage, where a memory is vague, malformed, or insufficiently actionable. For each case, we annotate the problematic components of the memory and explain why retrieving it may hurt downstream decision-making.

J.1.2 Additional examples

We further list additional abnormal memories selected by the LLM-as-judge from ScienceWorld memory banks. These examples are grouped into the same three categories: over_generalization, over_specialization, and useless_garbage.

J.1.3 Memory banks across consolidation rounds

We further examine the evolution of memory banks produced by GPT-5.4-mini in the ScienceWorld environment. The model performs 20 rounds of memory consolidation over 485 rollouts. We show three representative memory banks: the first round, which reflects the initial memory bank; the tenth round, which reflects an intermediate memory bank; and the twentieth round, which reflects the final memory bank. For each memory bank, we also report the corresponding average test score.

Appendix K Additional Analyses

K.1 Auto-Mode Component Ablation

The main-text Auto + Episodic curve in Fig. 9(b) couples two memory sources. To isolate their contributions we re-run evaluation at four checkpoints with each source restricted in turn: Abstract Only reads only the distilled abstract memory, Episodic Only reads only the raw episodic store, and Auto reads both. The Episodic Only condition recovers nearly all of the Auto gain; Abstract Only never improves on zero-shot (Fig. 17).

K.2 Memory Composition under Task Switching

Supporting evidence for the Fresh-vs-Cumulative comparison in §6.2. After each of the 15 ScienceWorld switch tasks, we ask an LLM judge to label every entry currently in the memory store as normal, over-generalized, over-specific, or garbage. Figure 18 plots the running totals of the two failure-mode categories (over-gen and garbage) across the sequence for GPT5.4-mini. Cumulative’s totals diverge from Fresh’s almost immediately and never recover, supplying a direct mechanistic account of the +203+203-point score gap reported in the main text.
